summaryEn: Sixty years of Taiwanese industry in one company: power cables for the national grid, stainless steel, Indonesian nickel mines, and founding stakes in Winbond, Walsin Technology, HannStar Board and HannStar Display. The operating businesses barely make money — and the headline quarterly profit came from elsewhere.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + Q1 2026 earnings call; conglomerate framing — the three-business structure, Indonesian nickel integration, Taipower grid demand and the founded affiliates credited, but the 2026Q1 EPS 0.81 headline dismantled: operating margin 1.33% versus 8.52% net margin, a NT$2.1bn FX gain, an undisclosed one-off disposal gain, equity-method income, a NT$5.6bn unrealised loss sitting below net income in OCI, and operating cash flow of -NT$3.33bn against +NT$3.50bn of reported profit; operating margin negative in three of six prior quarters and dividend cut from NT$1.8 to NT$0.5; sector 電器電纜 → Wire & Cable, Stainless Steel & Resources; nameZh 華新 → 華新麗華)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Walsin Lihwa (華新麗華, TWSE: 1605) is what sixty years of Taiwanese industrial expansion looks like assembled into one balance sheet. Founded in **1966** and **listed in November 1972**, it runs three operating businesses — **stainless steel** (back above half of revenue), **wire and cable** (steady at a 12% gross margin, and supplying Taiwan's national grid), and **resources**, meaning **nickel mining in Indonesia through Walsin Nickel**, which feeds its own stainless production. From 1980 it also **founded or seeded a series of electronics companies that are now listed in their own right**: **Winbond (2344)**, one of the world's larger DRAM suppliers; **Walsin Technology (2492)**, a global top-five MLCC maker; **HannStar Board (5469)** in printed circuit boards; and **HannStar Display (6116)** in LCD panels.

That structure explains both the appeal and the problem. **NT$306.2bn of assets and NT$174.5bn of equity** produce a **trailing return on equity of just 3.0%**, and the market values the whole thing at **0.83× book** — below the accounting value of its own assets. Annual EPS collapsed from **NT$5.42 (FY2022) to 1.32 (FY2023), 0.71 (FY2024) and NT$0.75 (FY2025)**, and the dividend was cut from **NT$1.8 to NT$1.1 to NT$0.5**, where it has stayed for two years. The yield is **1.63%**.

**The most recent quarter requires careful reading, and this page will not present it as a recovery.** 2026Q1 produced **EPS of NT$0.81 — more than the whole of FY2025** — on revenue of **NT$41.1bn, down 8.5% year-on-year**. But the **operating margin was 1.33% against a net margin of 8.52%**. The company's own disclosure identifies the difference: a **NT$2.1bn foreign-exchange gain** from a weakening New Taiwan dollar, an **undisclosed one-off gain on the disposal of an investment**, and **equity-method income from the electronics affiliates**. Below the net income line, the comprehensive income statement carried a **NT$5.6bn unrealised loss** on listed equity holdings whose market prices fell — a loss that does not touch reported earnings. And **operating cash flow was −NT$3.33bn** in the same quarter that reported **+NT$3.50bn of net profit**.

The operating businesses are genuinely improving — stainless losses narrowed sharply, resources margins rebounded on Indonesian nickel policy, and cable is supported by **Taipower's grid-resilience programme**. But **operating margin was negative in three of the prior six quarters**. The honest read: **a substantial, conservatively financed industrial group with real assets and real optionality — whose reported earnings have for years depended more on investments and currency than on the businesses it operates.**

Walsin Lihwa was founded in **1966**, at the start of the industrial build-out that transformed Taiwan. Its first business was the most basic input of an electrifying economy: **wire and cable**. Copper conductors carry power from generation to factories and homes, and a country building its grid, its industry and its cities needs enormous quantities of them. The company **listed in 1972**.

From that base it expanded in two directions at once. The first was **deeper into metals** — into **stainless steel**, producing billets, wire rod, bars and seamless tube, and then further upstream still into **resources**, establishing **Walsin Nickel** to secure nickel from **Indonesia**, the world's dominant source. Nickel is the essential alloying element in stainless steel; owning the mine means the group's largest input cost is partly internalised rather than bought at market. Vertical integration from ore to finished stainless is unusual for a Taiwanese company.

The second direction was **electronics**. From **1980**, Walsin Lihwa began founding and seeding technology companies, and these became substantial businesses in their own right: **Winbond (2344)** in memory, ranking among the world's larger DRAM suppliers; **Walsin Technology (2492)**, a global top-five maker of multilayer ceramic capacitors; **HannStar Board (5469)** in printed circuit boards; and **HannStar Display (6116)** in LCD panels. The Chiao family group that built Walsin thereby ended up spanning heavy industry and semiconductors simultaneously.

The consequence, six decades on, is a company whose **reported profits are only loosely connected to what it manufactures**. Equity-method income from the affiliates, gains on disposing of holdings, and currency translation on foreign operations can each exceed operating profit from cables, steel and nickel combined. That is not a criticism of the strategy — the electronics investments were prescient — but it makes Walsin Lihwa a company that must be read carefully, because **the headline earnings number frequently describes something other than the business.**

- **1966 (2 Dec)** — Walsin Lihwa founded, making **wire and cable** for Taiwan's electrifying economy.
- **1972 (3 Nov)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (1605)**.
- **1970s–1990s** — Expands into **stainless steel** — billets, wire rod, bars, seamless tube — and builds international production and sales operations.
- **From 1980** — Begins founding and seeding electronics companies: **Winbond (2344)**, **Walsin Technology (2492)**, **HannStar Board (5469)** and **HannStar Display (6116)**.
- **Resources era** — Establishes **Walsin Nickel** and invests in **Indonesian nickel** to secure the key stainless-steel input upstream.
- **2022** — Peak year: **EPS NT$5.42**; dividend **NT$1.8**.
- **2023** — Sharp fall: **EPS NT$1.32**; dividend cut to **NT$1.1**.
- **2024** — **EPS NT$0.71**, including a **loss in Q4 (−NT$0.15)** and a **−0.2% operating margin**; dividend cut again to **NT$0.5**.
- **2025** — **EPS NT$0.75**, with **operating margin negative in Q3 (−1.6%) and Q4 (−1.9%)**; dividend held at **NT$0.5**.
- **2026Q1** — Reported **EPS NT$0.81** — exceeding all of FY2025 — on revenue of **NT$41.1bn (−8.5% YoY)**. **Operating margin 1.33%, net margin 8.52%.** Contributors: a **NT$2.1bn FX gain**, an **undisclosed one-off disposal gain**, and equity-method income. A **NT$5.6bn unrealised loss** on listed equity holdings sits in comprehensive income, outside net profit. **Operating cash flow −NT$3.33bn.**

Walsin Lihwa's accounts are the clearest case in this collection of **reported earnings needing to be taken apart before they mean anything**.

- **A multi-year earnings collapse.** Annual EPS: **NT$5.42 (FY2022) → 1.32 (FY2023) → 0.71 (FY2024) → NT$0.75 (FY2025)** — an **86% fall from the peak**. Trailing **return on equity is 3.0%**.
- **The operating businesses have been losing money at the operating line.** Operating margin by quarter: **−0.2% (2024Q4), +2.1%, +1.1%, −1.6%, −1.9% (2025Q4), +1.3% (2026Q1)**. **Negative in three of the last six quarters.** Gross margin runs **4.8–8.2%** — commodity economics.
- **Now the important part: what 2026Q1 actually was.** Reported **EPS NT$0.81** — more than the whole of FY2025 — on revenue of **NT$41.1bn, down 8.5% year-on-year**. **Operating margin 1.33%; net margin 8.52%.** The company's own disclosure identifies the gap:
  - a **NT$2.1bn foreign-exchange gain** from translating overseas operations as the New Taiwan dollar weakened;
  - **a one-off gain on disposing of an investment holding** — described as contributing significantly to net profit, with **the amount not disclosed**;
  - **equity-method income** from the electronics affiliates.
  None of these is operating profit, and **none is repeatable by running the business better**.
- **The loss that does not appear in earnings.** The same quarter's comprehensive income statement carried a **NT$5.6bn unrealised loss** on listed equity investments held by Walsin and its equity-method affiliates, as their market prices fell. Because it sits in **other comprehensive income**, it never passes through the NT$3.60bn net profit — but it reduced shareholders' equity all the same.
- **Cash contradicted profit.** **Operating cash flow was −NT$3.33bn** in the quarter that reported **+NT$3.50bn of net income**. When profit and cash point in opposite directions by that margin, the profit is the number to question.
- **The dividend records the reality.** **NT$1.8 (FY2022) → 1.1 (FY2023) → NT$0.5 (FY2024 and FY2025)** — a **72% cut**, held down for two years. The **1.63% yield** is the lowest of any mature industrial company in this collection.
- **A large, under-worked balance sheet.** **NT$306.2bn of assets, NT$174.5bn of equity**, a conservative **43.0% debt ratio** and **NT$13.9bn of cash** — producing **3.0% ROE**. The market's response is a **0.83× price-to-book**: it values the company below the stated worth of its own assets.

The financing reality: **a well-capitalised group whose assets are real and whose operating returns are not** — with a headline quarter that looks like a turnaround and, on inspection, is mostly currency and a disposal.

**Stance: a sixty-year industrial group trading 17% below book value, with genuine operating improvement under way — and a reported profit that, quarter after quarter, comes from investments and currency rather than from operations.**

The bull case:

1. **Real assets bought below stated value.** **NT$174.5bn of equity** valued at **0.83× book**, with a conservative **43.0% debt ratio**. The holdings alone — founding stakes in **Winbond, Walsin Technology, HannStar Board and HannStar Display** — carry value independent of the industrial operations.
2. **The operating businesses are genuinely improving.** Management reported **stainless-steel losses narrowing markedly**, **resources margins rebounding sharply** on tighter Indonesian nickel policy and a new April auction mechanism, and **wire and cable holding a 12% gross margin** with demand from **Taipower's grid-resilience programme**. Guidance was for stainless and cable to improve further and resources to hold.
3. **Vertical integration into nickel** — an unusual position for a Taiwanese company, giving partial control over stainless steel's key input cost.
4. **Structural tailwinds** in the guidance: raw-material price rises, **Chinese export controls** and the **EU's CBAM carbon border mechanism** all favouring non-Chinese stainless supply.

The counter-arguments:

- **The headline profit is not operating profit.** 2026Q1's **NT$0.81 EPS** sat on a **1.33% operating margin**, with a **NT$2.1bn FX gain**, an **undisclosed disposal gain** and equity-method income making up the difference — while a **NT$5.6bn unrealised loss** sat below the line and **operating cash flow was −NT$3.33bn**.
- **The operating record is poor.** **Negative operating margin in three of six quarters**; gross margin of **4.8–8.2%**; **3.0% ROE** on NT$174.5bn of equity.
- **The dividend was cut 72%** and has stayed there.
- **Conglomerate opacity.** Earnings depend on affiliate results, disposal timing and currency — three things outside investors cannot forecast.

A **deep-value, low-conviction** thesis: real assets at a discount with improving operations — provided one values the balance sheet rather than the income statement.

Walsin Lihwa operates **three industrial businesses plus a portfolio of founding stakes**, and they earn money in quite different ways:

- **Stainless steel (back above 50% of revenue).** Billets, wire rod, bars and seamless tube, produced in Taiwan and internationally. This is a **commodity metals business**: margins are set by the spread between nickel and scrap input costs and stainless selling prices, and it has been **loss-making at the operating line**, with losses narrowing markedly in the most recent quarter as raw-material prices rose, Chinese export controls tightened and the **EU's CBAM carbon border mechanism** began favouring non-Chinese supply.
- **Wire and cable (steady, ~12% gross margin).** Power and communication cable, including for **Taipower's grid-resilience programme** — Taiwan's multi-year effort to harden its electricity network. This is the most predictable business: infrastructure demand, long qualification, domestic customers.
- **Resources — Indonesian nickel.** Through **Walsin Nickel**, the group mines nickel in Indonesia, the world's dominant source, and converts it into nickel pig iron. Nickel is stainless steel's essential alloying element, so this is **vertical integration into the group's own largest raw-material cost**. In 2026Q1, shipment volumes were low and revenue fell, yet **net profit was strong and gross margin rebounded sharply** as Indonesia tightened mining policy and a **new April auction mechanism pushed ore prices up**.
- **The affiliates.** Founding stakes in **Winbond (2344, memory)**, **Walsin Technology (2492, MLCC)**, **HannStar Board (5469, PCB)** and **HannStar Display (6116, panels)**, consolidated by the equity method — meaning their profits flow into Walsin's income statement without being operating income.

The economics are therefore **two businesses at once**. The industrial operations produce **4.8–8.2% gross margins** and an operating margin that has oscillated around zero. The investment portfolio produces **equity-method income, disposal gains and unrealised value changes** that regularly exceed operating profit. **In 2026Q1 the operating businesses generated a 1.33% margin while the reported net margin was 8.52%.**

The strength is genuine asset backing and vertical integration from ore to finished metal. The vulnerability is that **an investor cannot forecast the earnings**, because the largest components — affiliate profits, disposal timing and currency translation — are not driven by anything management does in the factories.

Walsin Lihwa competes in three industries at once, and each has its own structure.

- **Stainless steel: a Chinese-dominated commodity.** China produces more than half the world's stainless steel, and its exports have kept global prices under pressure for years — the reason Walsin's stainless division has been loss-making at the operating line. Two forces are now working the other way: **Chinese export controls** restricting outbound supply, and the **EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM)**, which prices the carbon content of imported steel and structurally disadvantages high-emission Chinese production. Both favour non-Chinese producers with cleaner processes.
- **Nickel: policy is the market.** Indonesia holds the world's dominant nickel reserves and has used export bans and licensing to force downstream processing onshore. Its policy decisions — **the tightening and the new April auction mechanism that raised ore prices** — move global nickel more than demand does. Walsin's Indonesian position converts that from a pure input risk into partly an earnings source.
- **Wire and cable: a domestic infrastructure business.** Competing with **Taiwan Cable, Ta Ya** and others, largely for **Taipower** and construction demand. Margins are modest but stable, and the **grid-resilience programme** provides a multi-year demand base — the same electricity-infrastructure theme visible at Fortune Electric elsewhere in this collection, though Walsin's exposure is far less concentrated.
- **The holding-company discount.** Markets routinely value diversified groups below the sum of their parts, because investors cannot buy the pieces they want, capital allocation is opaque, and reported earnings blend unrelated sources. **Walsin's 0.83× price-to-book** is that discount made explicit — and it is the central question in the investment case: whether the discount is unjustified, or an accurate assessment of a group earning **3.0% on equity**.

Walsin's position is **structurally defensible in cable, structurally challenged in stainless, and policy-dependent in nickel**. The industry truth is that **vertical integration from ore to metal is genuinely valuable when the metal earns a margin** — and Walsin's stainless division has only just stopped losing money.

**Strengths**
- **Vertical integration from Indonesian nickel to finished stainless** — partial control of the key input cost, unusual for a Taiwanese company.
- **Founding stakes in Winbond (2344), Walsin Technology (2492), HannStar Board (5469) and HannStar Display (6116)** — substantial listed assets independent of operations.
- **Wire and cable at a steady 12% gross margin**, supported by **Taipower's grid-resilience programme**.
- **Conservative balance sheet**: **43.0% debt ratio**, **NT$174.5bn of equity**, trading at **0.83× book**.

**Weaknesses**
- **Operating margin negative in three of the last six quarters**; gross margin only **4.8–8.2%**; **3.0% ROE**.
- **EPS down 86% from peak**: **NT$5.42 → 0.75**; dividend cut **NT$1.8 → NT$0.5**.
- **Reported profit driven by non-operating items** — 2026Q1's NT$0.81 EPS on a 1.33% operating margin.
- **Operating cash flow −NT$3.33bn** against +NT$3.50bn of reported net profit.

**Opportunities**
- **Chinese export controls and EU CBAM** favouring non-Chinese stainless supply.
- **Indonesian nickel policy tightening** supporting resource-segment margins.
- Taipower grid investment sustaining cable demand; discount to book closing if operations recover.

**Threats**
- **Chinese stainless overcapacity** resuming price pressure.
- **Indonesian policy reversal** removing the nickel price support.
- **Affiliate earnings and equity values falling** — a **NT$5.6bn unrealised loss** already recorded in one quarter.

- **The headline earnings figure is misleading (the most important risk for a reader).** 2026Q1 reported **EPS of NT$0.81 — more than all of FY2025** — but the **operating margin was 1.33% against an 8.52% net margin**. The difference came from a **NT$2.1bn currency gain**, an **undisclosed one-off gain on disposing of an investment**, and equity-method income from affiliates. Treating that quarter as evidence of operational recovery would be a straightforward error.
- **A large loss sits outside net income.** The same quarter carried a **NT$5.6bn unrealised loss** on listed equity holdings in **other comprehensive income**. It never touches reported earnings, but it reduces equity — and it will not appear in any EPS-based screen.
- **Cash flow contradicted profit.** **−NT$3.33bn of operating cash flow** against **+NT$3.50bn of net income** in the same quarter. Persistent divergence of that size is the standard warning sign that reported profit is not economic profit.
- **The operating businesses have barely been profitable.** **Negative operating margin in three of six recent quarters**, **gross margin of 4.8–8.2%**, and **3.0% return on equity** on **NT$174.5bn** of capital. The improvement is real but recent and unproven.
- **Policy dependence in two of three businesses.** Stainless improvement rests on **Chinese export controls and EU CBAM**; resource margins rest on **Indonesian mining policy**. Both are government decisions that can reverse.
- **Conglomerate opacity and the dividend.** Earnings blend operations, affiliates, disposals and currency, and the disposal gain's size was **not disclosed**. Meanwhile the dividend has been **cut 72% to NT$0.5** and held there — a **1.63% yield** offering little compensation for the complexity.

Walsin Lihwa's outlook rests on one question: **can the operating businesses earn a genuine margin, so that the reported profit stops depending on disposals and currency?** The axes to watch:

- **Operating margin — and nothing else on the income statement.** It has run **−0.2%, +2.1%, +1.1%, −1.6%, −1.9%, +1.3%** across six quarters. A sustained operating margin of several percent would be the first real change in years. **Net profit and EPS should be ignored until the operating line supports them.**
- **The stainless turnaround.** Losses narrowed markedly in 2026Q1, with management guiding Q2 better still on **rising raw-material prices, Chinese export controls and EU CBAM**. Stainless is back above **50% of revenue**, so this segment determines the group's operating result.
- **Indonesian nickel policy.** The resources segment's strong margins came from **tightened mining policy and a new April auction mechanism raising ore prices**, not from higher shipments — volumes actually fell. That makes the earnings policy-dependent and worth monitoring at source.
- **Cash flow versus profit.** After **−NT$3.33bn of operating cash flow against +NT$3.50bn of net income**, the convergence of those two lines is the single best test of whether an improvement is real.
- **The dividend.** Held at **NT$0.5** for two years after a **72% cut**. Restoring it would be management's own signal that operating earnings have returned.

Bottom line: Walsin Lihwa owns **real, integrated industrial assets — Indonesian nickel feeding stainless steel, cable supplying Taiwan's grid — plus founding stakes in Winbond, Walsin Technology, HannStar Board and HannStar Display**, financed conservatively at a **43.0% debt ratio** and priced at **0.83× book**. It is also a group earning **3.0% on equity**, with **negative operating margins in half of recent quarters**, an **86% fall in EPS from peak**, a **72% dividend cut**, and a headline quarter whose **NT$0.81 EPS rested on a 1.33% operating margin** alongside a **NT$5.6bn unrealised loss** and **negative operating cash flow**. Judge it on **operating margin and operating cash flow** — assets worth more than the market says, attached to operations that have not yet earned their keep.
